draft.title: Jewish environmental ethics
card: In Jewish teaching, the earth belongs to God. Psalm 24 says, "The earth is the Lord's and all that is in it." Humans use the earth but do not own it outright.
Because of this, people are seen as caretakers. Genesis 2 describes the first human placed in the garden "to work it and to keep it".
the rule against needless destruction. It comes from Deuteronomy 20, which forbids cutting down fruit trees when besieging a city. Rabbis later applied it to wasting things more widely.
Bal tashchit does not ban all use of resources. It rules out waste and harm that serve no purpose. Many Jews apply these ideas to issues such as pollution and climate change.
draft.remember: The earth is God's, so people care for it and avoid needless destruction.

a.q: Why do many Jews believe humans must care for the environment?
opts: The earth belongs to God, so humans are its caretakers
Humans own the earth, so they must protect their property
Nature is divine, so it must never be touched or used
The Torah bans humans from using any natural resources
a.why: Jewish teaching holds that the earth is God's and humans are entrusted with it as caretakers. Ownership by humans is the tempting wrong answer, because the card says people use the earth but do not own it outright.
a.clue: Think about who the earth belongs to.

b.q: Dani runs a bakery in Sydney and throws out large amounts of good food each day because he ordered too much. Which Jewish idea does this most clearly break?
opts: Bal tashchit, the rule against needless destruction
The ban on using any natural resources for business
The belief that humans own the earth outright
The command to cut down fruit trees in wartime
b.why: Throwing away good food for no purpose is needless waste, which bal tashchit rules out. The ban on all resource use is tempting but wrong, because the rule targets waste and harm without purpose, not all use.
b.clue: The rule is about waste that serves no purpose.

a.best: The earth belongs to God, so humans are its caretakers

b.best: Bal tashchit, the rule against needless destruction

problems.detail: The clue 'The rule is about waste that serves no purpose' restates the right option's gloss ('the rule against needless destruction'), so students can match words without understanding the idea.
The distractors are implausible for Year 12 HSC. A 'command to cut down fruit trees' reverses the card, and the other two contradict it outright, so only one option is credible.

b.q: Dani runs a bakery in Sydney. He throws out lots of good bread each day because he orders too much. A rabbi says this breaks bal tashchit. Which reasoning best supports the rabbi?
opts: Rabbis extended the rule to pointless waste of any kind
Deuteronomy 20 names food waste alongside fruit trees
Bal tashchit forbids using resources to make a profit
Humans may not consume anything that belongs to God
b.why: The verse in Deuteronomy 20 is about fruit trees in a siege, but rabbis later applied it to waste more widely, so throwing out good bread for no reason falls under it. The profit option is tempting, but bal tashchit does not ban using resources, and baking bread to sell is a real purpose.
b.clue: Compare what the original verse covers with how it was later applied.

a.best: The earth belongs to God, so humans are its caretakers

b.best: Rabbis extended the rule to pointless waste of any kind
